content.thinking:
For Warcraft-style, there's no explicit kit, so I'll go hand-painted rather than cel-shaded, using paint techniques like gradient, mottle, grain, scales, and stripes. I should peek at the sample directory and meta example for reference.

Now I'm sketching the design: a chunky dwarf around 1.25-1.3m tall with a big head, huge shoulders and hands, short legs, wearing a brimmed hat with brass goggles, braided beard with brass rings, heavy riveted pauldrons, a bandolier with powder horn and shot pouches, a wide belt buckle, kilt-like coat, and heavy boots, holding a blunderbuss with a flared brass muzzle and flintlock mechanism in a readable A-pose rest stance.

For the pose I'm deciding the right hand grips the blunderbuss at the stock, held forward-up at an angle away from the body so it doesn't intersect, while the left arm rests open in a relaxed A-pose position; I'll keep the hands simplified rather than fully articulated fingers to save on complexity.

For the gripping hand I'll wrap finger paths around the weapon's grip cylinder. Now I'm sizing the overall proportions: a stout dwarf around 1.3m tall with hat, following heroic Warcraft style with an oversized head and massive torso.

I'm plotting the vertical layout from feet to head: boots at the base with a short ankle rise, knees around 0.36, hips at 0.55-0.6 given short legs, waist near 0.68, chest and shoulders around 0.95-1.05, neck at 1.1, and a large head centered near 1.18 with the hat extending the total height toward 1.35-1.4.

Now I'm adjusting proportions down slightly for a stockier dwarf build, setting shoulder width wide for pauldrons, a barrel chest, and a big belly, then starting to define the skeleton hierarchy -- root hips joint, spine chain curving up through chest to neck base using a catmull spline.

Setting up the joint hierarchy...

I'm figuring out how the beard should attach—mustache under the jaw, main beard mass rigid to the jaw so it moves with mouth opening, while braids hang as chains of three joints rooted on the head for a nicer dangling rig.

Then I'm moving to the arms, placing the shoulder, elbow, and hand joints for an A-pose, deciding on shorter forearm proportions with a larger hand for the limb chain.

Right arm positioning for the blunderbuss: shoulder, elbow, and wrist placed so the forearm angles forward to grip the weapon, with the stock tucked near the hip and butt under the arm while the barrel points forward and slightly up, sized a bit larger than real-world scale to suit the heroic dwarf proportions.

I'm working through the hand and barrel placement to avoid the stock colliding with the elbow, nudging the weapon's axis further outward and adjusting the wrist and elbow coordinates to keep everything clear of the body.

Simplest solution: hold the blunderbuss in the right hand pointed slightly forward, outward, and up at A-pose side, defining it in a local coordinate frame with the barrel along +Z and origin at the grip, then transforming into world space using the aim quaternion so all the weapon's parts follow consistently.

I think building the weapon mostly from rods, sweeps, and lathes with a transformed world basis will work well—rods for shafts, lathe for barrel bells, with a helper function to place parts using world-space position and combined quaternion rotation.

Now I'm defining the weapon's local coordinate basis: forward along the barrel (z), up (y), and left (x) derived from up crossed with forward, giving a right-handed system matching the model convention. Then I start sketching the blunderbuss design in these local coordinates, laying out the wooden stock from the butt back near z=-0.34 up to the wrist near the grip.

Working out stock profile points...

Continuing the stock outline down through the wrist underside and forward to the fore-stock, then up over the comb to the heel, giving it a 0.05 wood-slab thickness with a small bevel. Next I'm shaping how the hand wraps around the wrist.

Simplifying to a Warcraft-style mitten fist: a palm block with four curled finger capsules wrapping around the stock's wrist treated as a rounded grip cylinder, with fingers curling around it in the plane perpendicular to the wrist's axis.

I'm thinking through the finger curve placement across z offsets, treating the grip like wrapping a fist around a horizontal pole—fingers starting at the back knuckle side and curling under toward the front, since the stock's wrist axis runs roughly along the barrel rather than vertical like a pistol grip.

Checking the elbow-wrist geometry, the forearm runs forward along z while gripping that same z-axis pole, which feels more like a hammer grip than a pistol wrist. I'm reconsidering whether to simplify by treating this as a tilted pistol-grip orientation instead, with the axis angled down and back roughly 30° from vertical, and the forearm approaching from behind.

I'm now placing the pistol grip itself below the lock, hanging down and back with a defined width, and setting the hand center position relative to it so fingers can wrap around the vertical grip in the x-z plane -- palm toward the rear, fingers curling forward, with the forearm approaching from the right-rear side at the hip.

This feels more natural: forearm aligned with the barrel behind the grip, like a typical rifle-hold, with the wrist positioned slightly back from the grip center and the fist wrapping around the front.

Trying to pin down the actual coordinates though — checking elbow and wrist positions against the weapon's grip point and barrel axis, I'm running into inconsistencies where the stock line seems to overlap with the forearm position instead of running clear behind it.

Let me rework the weapon's tilt instead: angle the barrel upward about 30° so the butt drops down and back near the hip rather than through the elbow, giving a heroic "ready" stance with the muzzle rising forward and up clear of the body.

I'm reconsidering centering the fist grip on the pistol grip and letting the arm angle outward slightly, accepting minor stock-forearm overlap since the forearm acts like a wrist guard. I'll try shifting the weapon axis so the forearm runs along its right side, checking stock half-width clearance against forearm position.

Rather than keep fine-tuning numbers theoretically, I decide to lock in a grip center point and forward vector for the weapon frame, planning to verify the pose visually with a preview render instead of over-deliberating further.

Still writing weapon geometry...

Still shaping the bell profile points...

I'm deciding to paint by checking whether the surface normal points toward the axis—if it does, it's the dark interior, otherwise brass. Then I'm adding reinforcing bands as torus rings at a few points along the barrel, and starting on the flintlock plate detail.

Next I'll build out the lock mechanism with its hammer, pan, and frizzen in brass, plus a swept trigger guard and small trigger below the grip. For the stock I'm extruding the wood slab with grain coloring, adding a brass butt plate, fore-stock ramrod pipes with the rod itself, and skipping the sling strap for simplicity—finishing with some scrollwork engraving on the brass and a rune decal on the barrel.

Now I'm turning to the dwarf character itself, settling on a warm ruddy skin tone with a copper-red braided beard accented in gold, paired with a deep navy coat trimmed in gold, brown leather, steel-gray pauldrons with brass rivets, and a brown hat with a red feather for contrast. I'm starting to lay out the head geometry as a scaled sphere with specific dimensions and positioning for the heroic proportions.

For facial features, I'm planning a heavy brow ridge, bulbous nose with bridge, and small sunken eyes under the brow, using tiny white and iris spheres or an SVG decal of a Warcraft-style eye with almond shape, light blue iris, dark ring, pupil, and heavy lid shading applied as a texture decal onto the skull. I'm also adding pointy rounded ears and chubby cheek spheres to round out the face.

For the mustache and beard, I'm sweeping a big handlebar mustache along catmull curves from under the nose that curls outward and up at the ends, plus a massive beard mass down to the belt with two thick side braids made from alternating sphere and capsule "plait" segments ending in brass beads, and possibly a third central braid, all painted with grain-like strand striping.

Now I'm thinking through the hat — considering a Warcraft rifleman-style wide-brimmed felt hat with one side pinned up with a brass badge and feather, versus a riveted steel kettle-helmet with plume, settling on the brimmed felt design built from a lathed crown and brim disk with separate extruded/rotated plates forming the upturned flap.

Rethinking the tricorn shape: the point should face forward with three corners folded upward at 0°, 120°, and 240°, so I'm placing the three corner panels at those azimuths.

Actually, let me simplify to a tricorn hat built from three trapezoid extrusions, giving a wide cavalry brim with the front peaked and one side folded up and pinned with a brass brooch and plume.

I realize the real tricorn shape has pointed corners projecting outward with the sides folded up against the crown, so I should add a small brim ring near the crown plus three projecting corner panels shaped like upturned leaf forms to capture that silhouette.

For finishing touches I'm adding a hat band with a gold buckle and a feather made from crossed curved plume cards for texture. I'm debating whether the hat is overdesigned, but decide it reads well as a rifleman character and skip any brim tilt for simplicity. Moving to the torso, I'll loft it through spine stations with varying hip and belly widths using a bone chain and catmull interpolation between station centers.

Sketching out station widths and depths for pelvis, waist, chest, shoulders, and neck base, bound to a hip/spine bone chain, then layering a blue padded coat with gold trim over it, leaving the forearms bare with leather bracers in classic dwarf-warrior style.

For arm detail I'm keeping short coat sleeves on the upper arm transitioning to skin with brass-studded bracers below, plus heavy symmetrical steel pauldrons domed and rimmed in gold with rivets. I'm adding a leather bandolier from right shoulder to left hip holding brass cartridge cylinders, and a wide belt with a brass rune-decorated buckle and pouches.

Now I'm working on hip gear: two flap-stitched pouches, a curved brass-tipped powder horn, a canteen, and a lathe-built skirt of leather tassets flaring down to the knees for the long coat tails. For legs, I'm laying out thick dark trousers, big cuffed boots with brass toe caps and buckled straps, and defining the joint chain from hip to knee to ankle for each leg.

For the feet, I'm adding a separate toe joint parented to the ankle so the boot can bend naturally, then building the boot itself from a frustum-shaped shaft sweeping up from ankle to shin, an elliptical loft for the forefoot extending to the toe, and a flat extruded sole slab underneath.

For the hands, I'm scaling them up with a palm block and four capsule-shaped fingers chained in segments, then wrapping a studded leather gauntlet cuff around the wrist, with the left hand posed slightly curled as if holding something small.

I'm tallying up the total joint count across hips, spine, neck, head, clavicles, arms, fingers, legs, and braids to make sure the rig stays manageable at around 55 joints, and planning to derive the right wrist position directly from the weapon's grip point so the hand wraps naturally around it.

Still working out finger wrap geometry...

Working out positions...

Still working out finger joint names and counts, then I'm defining the stock grip as a wood rod running down from the palm, and sketching the thumb's wrap path along the left side of the grip for a right-hand hold.

Now I'm turning to the left hand, which hangs freely in an A-pose with slightly curled fingers and the palm facing inward, planning out its joint positions.

Now I'm setting the left wrist position and palm box dimensions, then planning the skin and beard paint treatments—mottled skin tones with blush accents, and copper-colored grain stripes for the beard with darker roots and braid rings.

Still defining material palettes...

This gives a painterly warm-top, cool-shadow effect with added height-based darkening for the legs to suggest occlusion. I'm keeping triangle counts low and sticking to a chunky, smooth low-poly style rather than hard facets, then moving into coding the actual body parts starting with the hips as the root joint.

For the legs, I'm mirroring left and right chains—hip, knee, ankle, toe—with slightly offset positions for a natural stance, marking them as "leg" roles with ground contact points and a hinge-style toe joint. I'm now working out the trousers as a swept mesh following the leg chain with tapering radius, choosing a dark charcoal-blue for the trousers and brown leather for the boots while staying within the limited flat color palette.

For the boots, I'm making the shaft rigid on the ankle bone since it sits below the knee joint, keeping it simple with a tapered rod shape rather than a full articulated sweep, then starting to loft the toe box geometry for the boot's foot section.

Thinking through bone weighting, I'll split the boot into two parts: the heel/instep rigged to the ankle bone, and a separate toe-box piece tied to the toe bone, so the front of the boot can flex independently.

For the sole, I'm extruding the outline in two sections as well—rear portion on the ankle bone, front portion on the toe bone—accepting a slight seam for simplicity. Moving on to the coat and torso, I'll loft them with painted color, then build the kilt as a lathed shape flaring from the hips down, widening slightly toward the front, though I realize the lathe function doesn't support per-axis scaling so I'll need another approach for that oval taper.

Rather than fighting the lathe limitation, I'll construct the skirt from around ten hanging trapezoidal panels arranged in a ring around the hips—tassets styled like plated leather with brass studs and gold trim for a Warcraft aesthetic. Each panel gets positioned around an elliptical radius with an outward-tilted extrusion direction so they flare naturally, using tangent vectors for the width axis and a downward-and-outward vector for the panel's length.

For the belt, I'm considering a swept tube loop around the hips, but since the torso cross-section is elliptical rather than circular, I need to figure out the right frame orientation for the sweep—possibly simpler to approximate as a scaled lathe ring instead and adjust its part scale to match the body's ellipticity.

I'm planning to assemble the full character piece by piece mentally, writing helper functions for vectors and cylinder geometry, and merging rivet/stud meshes from sphere geometry attached to specific bones like the pauldron, before running a typecheck and preview pass.

For the pauldrons, I'm designing a lathe-based half-dome shape tilted outward over each shoulder, working out the outline points for the dome profile and planning a steel finish with a gold rim detail near the base.

I'm layering this further with stacked lame rings beneath the main dome, considering a brass boss on top and rivet spheres around the rim, and attaching the whole assembly to the shoulder joint bone so it moves naturally with the arm.

For the arm itself, I'm sweeping a single mesh along the limb that transitions from blue sleeve coloring on the upper arm to bare skin on the forearm, tapering the radius toward the elbow and wrist for a stocky dwarf build, then adding a leather bracer cuff as a separate sweep over part of the forearm.

I'm defining the bracer radius as slightly larger than the underlying forearm radius function so it reads as a wrapped cuff, and considering small details like brass studs or a rune tattoo decal for character. For the hands, I'm figuring out how to construct the palm shape, maybe using a box-based approach with rounded edges.

Now I'm working through fingerless rifleman gloves: leather covering the palm and finger bases, with bare skin at the fingertips using a color band split partway along each finger. Then I'm moving into the face, scaling the head sphere, placing it, and setting up a brow sweep with a curved bar and bushy orange brow color before getting into the eyes.

Adding facial features: a ruddy nose sphere, blush-painted cheek spheres, a small scar decal over the left eye for dwarf warrior character, and pointed ears with a brass ring earring. For the eyes, I'm crafting an SVG decal with an almond-shaped white sclera, dark upper lid line, blue-gray iris with ring and pupil, and highlight, positioning it using spherical coordinates on the skull surface mirrored for each side.

Now I'm sketching curved mustache sweeps that curl upward at the tips using tapered loft paths in beard-colored material, then building the beard as a wedge-shaped loft running from ear to ear under the chin, wide at the top and narrowing to a point near the bottom.

For positioning, I need the beard to rest properly on the chest, which protrudes forward to about z=0.18 at the torso front, so I'm adjusting the beard stations to sit at z≥0.2 — starting wide at the chin and tapering down in width and depth toward the lower chest, planning to check the fit visually once rendered.

Now I'm thinking through texture: scattering hair-tuft cards (around 120-150) across the beard surface with copper highlighting for a fibrous look, tilted along the downward flow. For braids, I'm planning two side braids starting near the cheeks and hanging down the chest, built from chained ellipsoid segments following a sweeping path with alternating rotation to create a plaited appearance.

Building the braid from the joint chain, using it as the path source for placing parts with inherited bone weights so the geometry can bend smoothly along the sweep.

I'll cap the braid core at a small radius to avoid gaps, finishing the end with a brass ring, cone tuft, and gold bead. I'm skipping extra mustache or side braids, but adding a bushy ponytail swept from under the hat at the back of the head, rigged to the head bone rather than its own joint chain.

For the hat, I'm checking total height: head top around 1.25, crown base at 1.2 rising to 1.31, with a feather pushing total height to about 1.43 -- close to the 1-1.4 m target for a dwarf, so I may trim the feather slightly.

Now I'm working out the arm rig: positioning a left clavicle joint at the chest aiming toward the shoulder, then defining the left arm chain through shoulder, elbow, and wrist points to set the upper arm length.

I'm now computing the right arm's mirrored positions and working out the weapon grip geometry, deriving the forward vector, orthogonalized up vector, and cross product to establish the hand's local coordinate frame relative to the grip point.

That's close to 0.225, good. Checking the upper arm length from shoulder to elbow gives 0.229, slightly shorter than the left side's 0.244 — minor asymmetry, probably not critical for rigging, so I'll nudge the elbow position slightly to even things out.

Now checking the forearm length and hand orientation — the right hand tip tangent looks correctly aimed forward-outward. I'm also checking clearance between the weapon's butt end and the elbow joint, computing the stock position in world space and comparing it against the elbow location — distance comes out around 0.14, which seems reasonable.

Checking the forearm midpoint against the stock position too — distances are small but acceptable since it's near the hand grip zone where some overlap is expected. Left arm and elbow look clear, so now I'm setting up the right hand geometry, defining the palm center and wrist position in weapon-local coordinates with the grip axis running vertically.

Working out the pistol grip shape as a cylinder, then placing finger positions along it with regular spacing, and checking the curl radius of each finger around the grip axis to make sure they wrap naturally around the handle.

Tracing the finger wrap path, I'm picturing the curve going from the rear point around the right side, to the front, and finally to the left — this matches a right hand gripping with palm behind and fingers curling rightward around to the front and left side.

Still refining finger joint angles...

Rethinking the scale for the dwarf's blunderbuss, I'll shrink the overall weapon length to fit a 1.3m tall dwarf — setting the breech tang near z=-0.30, barrel running to z=0.30, and the bell flare opening from 0.30 to 0.52.

Now I'm sketching the stock geometry: placing the lock and foregrip positions, adding barrel bands, and working out the outline points for the butt, wrist, and pistol grip as a polygon in z-y coordinates.

I'm reworking the grip as a separate rod rather than part of the outline, defining its axis with a slight backward tilt and figuring out where the finger-wrap circles should sit along it, along with positioning the trigger guard just forward of the grip.

Then I'm computing the wrist joint's world position by transforming its local offset through the local axes, and using that to recheck the forearm segment length between elbow and wrist, confirming it comes out close to the expected limb length.

Now I'm sketching the stock outline as a series of z,y coordinate points tracing the bottom profile from butt through wrist to the forestock, then checking the barrel's vertical position to make sure the forestock top sits just below the barrel, and continuing the outline along the top edge back toward the butt to close the shape.

Thickness and bevel values are set for the stock, and I'm planning a thin brass butt plate extruded from a trapezoid outline at the rear, plus a lock plate shape on the right side extruded from an elongated outline with a tail toward the front.

Now I'm sketching the cock/hammer as a curved steel sweep tapering from the jaw down to the pivot, with a small pan box near the touch hole on the barrel's left side, and I'll add simple cylindrical discs for the screws while skipping a detailed frizzen for now.

Next I'm building the brass trigger guard as a looping sweep around the trigger area with a small spike-shaped trigger inside it, then laying out the steel barrel as a tapered octagonal sweep with a breech tang cap, brass decorative rings along its length, and a flared muzzle bell at the end -- followed by starting work on the ramrod positioned beneath the barrel.

Now I'm adding rectangular brass bands wrapping the forestock as flattened boxes rather than full torus rings, then sketching a leather sling strap as a sagging curve looping from the forestock down past the hip to the butt for added realism and mass.

I'm checking that the sling path clears the hand/grip region, since the fingers only extend to about y=-0.08 while the strap dips lower. For decoration, I'm planning gold scroll inlay decals as transparent-textured plane geometries mounted flush against both sides of the stock.

I'm also sketching out other embellishments: a maker's rune plate on the barrel, small gold tally marks on the stock for kill count, and glove cuffs/bracers. For the torso coat, I'm using position-based painting to add a gold vertical trim stripe down the front placket, brass button studs along both sides, and a lathe-turned upturned collar with gold piping.

Now I'm skipping the tabard and instead draping a bandolier strap diagonally across the chest, defining a closed loop of points over the right shoulder, across the front, around the left hip, and back around to create the strap path.

Still placing cartridge vials...

Sticking cylinders outward using surface normals would make the vials jut out like a belt, but that's wrong—real bandolier vials sit upright in loops, not protruding perpendicular from the body.

I'm settling on vertical cylinders positioned along the strap, each oriented world-up with brass cap spheres on top, offset slightly outward so they read as a row of bandolier vials.

For the back, I'm adding a leather backpack box, a horizontal bedroll cylinder with straps on top, and a hanging canteen to round out the high-detail silhouette.

For accessories I'm placing hip pouches on the belt, a curved powder horn hanging at the left hip with a strap along the thigh, and a feather plus badge on the hat for extra character detail.

Adding a tankard with a handle for that dwarf flavor. I'm also planning the SVG texture assets needed: eye texture, gold scroll decal for the stock, beard-hair tuft cards, feather cards, and rune decals for the buckle, tattoo, and other details, while keeping total part count under a thousand.

I'm sketching a generic pauldron emblem (a gold chevron/star rune to avoid any trademarked logos), plus a belt buckle with a rune decal and a hat badge, and thinking through adding a small glowing ruby gem accent on the hat badge or lock.

Setting up the import scaffolding...

Now I'm defining the color palette: warm skin tones, fiery beard shades, blue coat colors, and gold accents for details.

I'll settle on a greenish-gray "#5a4f46" for trousers to pair with the coat and steel tones. Now I'm defining a leather paint helper that applies mottled shading between the leather colors with some scuffing texture.

For the torso, I'm lofting a sequence of cross-sections from hips to shoulders, each specifying a width and height at increasing heights along the body, bound to the hip and spine bones with the coat color -- building the coat's silhouette from narrow waist to broad chest and tapering shoulders.

Checking the shoulder width at y=0.97, roughly ±0.27, against the shoulder joint at ±0.29 so arms sit slightly outside with pauldrons covering the seam. Comparing chest width to head size gives a heroic proportion. For the neck I'm sweeping a thin skin-colored tube along a short curved path up to the head joint, but stacking up the head position, hat height, and torso top makes the total height run taller than intended, so I need to compress the leg and neck segments to bring the proportions back in line.

Working through the exact y-coordinates for the head sphere, jaw, neck chain, and hat crown to get the height under control, then recalculating shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions for the arms and the hip-knee-ankle stations for the short dwarf legs. With all these station heights tuned, I'm ready to start writing the actual model code.

I'm now positioning the skirt panels around the torso, placing the ring of panels in an ellipse shape at the waist and making sure the front panels flare outward enough to clear the thighs without clipping into them.

Adding gold trim paint logic...

Computing the outward normal for the tilt, then making the back coat panels longer at 0.32. For the belt, I'm working out a surface loop around the torso at a lifted height to wrap it properly around the body.

Right, radius [r0,r1] is just a linear taper, not an ellipse, so I'll use a constant function returning the fixed box dimensions instead. For the buckle I'm placing a brass frustum box near the front with a gold rune decal, then continuing with a stud placed along the belt.

I need to figure out where the belt sits relative to the torso's waist ellipse, then raycast against the torso surface to find the correct buckle position rather than guessing coordinates. Now I'm moving on to the head construction, defining the skull sphere's scale and position so its front face lines up at the right depth, then working out the jaw joint placement.

I'm positioning the lower jaw, nose, and brow ridge using sphere and sweep primitives with specific coordinates and radii, including bushy eyebrow tufts with a copper tone.

For the eyebrows I'm giving them a slight angry slope rather than straight bars, with inner points lower and outer points higher for a stern dwarven look. I'm then working out where the sunken eyes sit just below the protruding brow, calculating the exact elevation so the eye decals rest correctly against the skull surface.

Next I'm placing cheekbone spheres, ears, and the hat, then building the hair underneath with sideburn masses and a back hair mass in a copper tone. For the beard I'm lofting it starting from the lower cheeks so it doesn't intersect the face, with the mustache hovering just above, and I'm working through the station widths and heights for the first loft point.

Still laying out beard stations...

I'm checking whether the beard geometry stays clear of the torso at each height, and deciding to rig the beard to the jaw bone so it follows jaw motion while the mustache stays on the head, with braids and chains also parented to the jaw.

Now I'm positioning three hanging braids off the front of the beard — left, center, right — tracing their path down past the belt line and checking they clear the skirt panel in front rather than clipping through it.

Realizing the center braid would collide with the belt buckle, I'm reworking it to two side braids at x=±0.06 instead, each with ring ties and tips ending above the belt, while keeping a separate central beard tuft hanging lower. I'm double-checking the buckle's width and depth against the braid positions to make sure they clear its edges in z.

Still writing braid chain geometry...

Still working out the frame placement...

I'm sketching the mustache as a sweep along a catmull curve attached to the head bone, with the hat details to fill in later and no pose needed for the jaw. For tri budget I'll keep sweeps at 8 sides, then start drawing SVG shapes for eye details using a curved path fill.

Writing scroll curve, then starting a tapered beard tuft shape...

Adding the feather shape now, drawing the quill line and crimson vane curves with their own highlight stroke.

For the buckle rune, I'm sketching a sun-and-chevron emblem in gold outline circle with simple cross lines, meant to echo a generic dwarven mark. I'm also considering a small blue-black tattoo band on the forearm as an optional decal detail.

Now I'm setting up the coordinate utilities for weapon placement, building a basis from forward, up, and left vectors anchored at an origin offset, so I can convert local weapon-space coordinates into world positions.

Writing part orientation helper...

The weapon needs to reference the wrist joint, so I need to build arms and compute the wrist position before creating the weapon parts. I'm also mapping the right hand fingers so their chain parents correctly to the wrist joint, working out the path coordinates from the weapon's local frame into world space.

Now I'm setting up each finger as a small catmull-rom chain parented to the wrist, then sweeping each with a tapered radius profile. For the left hand, I'm computing the wrist position and forearm direction vector to orient the palm and fingers so they hang naturally with a slight curl.

I'm defining the hand's hanging direction vector, placing the palm box offset along it, and sizing the box's thin/width/length dimensions relative to the body-facing axis so it reads correctly in local coordinates.

For the fingers, I'm computing knuckle positions spread along the local Z axis derived from the hand's orientation quaternion, then building each finger as a short curved path from the knuckle outward with a slight forward bend, giving the middle fingers a touch more length for a natural curl.

For the thumb, I'm anchoring it near the front-top of the palm and curving it forward and slightly inward to match a hanging hand with the palm facing the body, which is anatomically correct for thumbs pointing forward.

I'm also setting up the glove styling with brass-studded leather knuckles, a wrist bracer cuff, and a thicker forearm radius, then starting the arm radius sweep function that will vary thickness along the upper arm.

Now I'm tapering the sleeve radius smoothly from shoulder to wrist with the elbow around the midpoint, adding a thin gold cuff ring near the elbow by sweeping a slightly larger radius over a short segment, making sure that cuff radius stays just outside the base arm radius function at that point.

I'm mirroring the same tapered sleeve and cuff setup for the right arm, then adding small armored elbow caps as scaled spheres positioned outward at each elbow joint, with rivets for a Warcraft-style armored look. I'm also setting up bone/joint naming for the wrist and clavicle so the arm chain parents correctly, and preparing to write out the full implementation now.

Moving to the legs, I'm sweeping a trouser chain from hip to knee to ankle with tapering radii, coloring it with a subtle mottled cloth texture, and adding steel-domed knee pads trimmed in gold using a lathe shape. I'm also starting the boot shaft as a rigid swept rod anchored at the ankle.

Now I'm shaping the boot cuff with a short folded ring in lighter leather and gold trim, sizing the tall chunky boot shaft so trousers tuck neatly inside, then lofting the boot foot from heel through arch to toe with varying section widths and heights along the path.

Still shaping sole outline...

I'm deciding to keep the toe joint simple by not splitting it, assigning the toe-cap parts there, while splitting the sole itself into back and front extrudes along a shared edge near z=0.07.

Now I'm setting the outline coordinates for both sole pieces and splitting the boot upper loft into heel and toe segments that share station 2 to hide the seam. For foot details I'm planning leather straps across the instep with a brass buckle, and considering a torus loop around the shaft to represent another strap with its own buckle.

Adding a brass toe cap sphere, then moving into the hat code, starting with the crown's lathe profile anchored above the head bone.

Picking a dark brown felt for the hat to contrast against the blue coat, with a gold band and red feather accent. Still writing the brim ring geometry and tricorn panel outlines...

Adding the hat band as a torus ring around the crown, sized to match the head and crown proportions.

I need to check that the hat fits properly over the skull by comparing radii at the crown base height, confirming the brim ring clears the head. Then I'm planning a small brass badge with a ruby gem to sit on the front of the crown surface.

For feathers, I'm positioning card frames on the left side of the hat angled outward and upward, using several overlapping cards with slight variation to simulate a feather cluster, double-sided so they read from any angle. For the hair, I'll use copper-toned sphere masses for the back hair mass and ears, then move on to writing the actual file with careful attention to TypeScript option types for the decal surface calls.

Now I'm working through beard cards scattered across the beard surface loft, filtering by normal direction to avoid stray placements, tuning the flow vector so the tufts hang downward naturally rather than using the default orientation. For coat details, I'm placing brass button studs along the torso centerline by raycasting from in front of the body inward to find the surface hit points at a few vertical positions.

Since the chest buttons would mostly be hidden by the beard, I'm dropping that idea and instead adding decorative gold piping and trim painted directly onto the torso texture -- gold bands near the hem and vertical lines along the front panel edges where the surface normal faces forward, accepting that the beard will cover much of it anyway.
